questions.q: What does a sparse autoencoder (SAE) do to a layer's activations?
options: It encodes them into a much wider, sparse hidden representation, then decodes back to the original dimension, aiming for a more monosemantic basis
It deletes most of the activations to save memory
It compresses them into fewer dimensions than the original layer
It replaces the model's weights entirely
questions.explain: An SAE deliberately expands into more directions than the original layer has, the opposite of compression, so each resulting direction can correspond to one coherent feature.

questions.q: What did "Towards Monosemanticity" find when it trained an SAE on a one-layer transformer's 512-neuron layer?
options: It found that the layer had zero interpretable structure of any kind
It found exactly 512 features, identical to the number of neurons
It reduced the layer down to a single feature
It decomposed the layer into more than 4,000 learned features, many more interpretable than the raw neurons
questions.explain: The SAE expanded 512 neurons into over 4,000 features covering specific, interpretable concepts like DNA sequences and legal language.

questions.q: What did "Scaling Monosemanticity" demonstrate, as described in this lesson?
options: That production-scale models contain no features for abstract concepts
That sparse autoencoders have no practical scaling properties at all
That the SAE technique only works on toy, one-layer models and fails on production models
That the same SAE approach scales to a production model (Claude 3 Sonnet), finding features like a "Golden Gate Bridge" feature and features tied to sycophancy and deception
questions.explain: Scaling Monosemanticity trained an SAE with tens of millions of features on Claude 3 Sonnet's residual stream and found both concrete and abstract interpretable features.

questions.q: In the SAE loss function `recon_loss + l1_coeff * sparsity_loss`, what would happen if the L1 term were removed entirely?
options: The SAE could learn an arbitrary, dense re-encoding that reconstructs well but isn't any more interpretable than the original neurons, since nothing pushes hidden features toward sparsity
The model's own weights would be permanently changed
Removing the L1 term would have no effect on the SAE's behavior
The SAE would fail to reconstruct the activations at all
questions.explain: Reconstruction loss alone doesn't require sparse, one-feature-per-unit codes; the L1 penalty is specifically what pushes most hidden units toward zero for any given input.

questions.q: Why is an SAE's hidden dimension (`d_hidden`) set much larger than the original activation dimension (`d_model`)?
options: Larger hidden dimensions are required by the PyTorch `nn.Linear` API
To match the model's vocabulary size exactly
To give the decomposition enough directions that it doesn't need to pack multiple features into one, the way the original model's superposed neurons do
To reduce the total number of parameters in the SAE
questions.explain: The expansion factor gives the SAE room to assign roughly one direction per feature instead of overlapping several features into one direction, as superposition does.
